name: Certified Implementation Specialist – Data Foundations (CMDB and CSDM)
note: ServiceNow does not publish a cut score for CIS-DF; community consensus puts it near 70%. Treat 85% here as your readiness bar. Items marked release-sensitive reference features, defaults, and CSDM terms that shift between releases; verify them against your own instance.

questions.stem: Where should an implementer define the identification rule, attributes, and health inclusion rules for a CI class?
options: In the System Dictionary only
In a business rule on the class table
In CI Class Manager
In the Discovery schedule
questions.explanation:
CI Class Manager is the central place to manage a class: hierarchy, attributes, identification and reconciliation rules, dependent relationships, and health settings. Using it keeps class configuration consistent and visible.

Business rules and direct dictionary edits bypass that structure. Discovery schedules control when discovery runs, not how classes are defined.

questions.stem: An organization needs to track a new type of infrastructure device with a few unique attributes. What is the recommended approach?
options: Create a standalone custom table for the devices that does not extend cmdb_ci
Add the new attributes directly to the cmdb_ci base table so every class can use them
Track the devices in a spreadsheet attached to a parent CI and update it each quarter
Extend the closest existing CI class so it inherits attributes, identification, and rules
questions.explanation:
Extending the closest existing class keeps the new type inside the CMDB hierarchy, so it inherits identification, health, and relationship behavior and works with features that expect CMDB classes.

Standalone tables lose all CMDB capability. Adding fields to the base cmdb_ci table pollutes every class.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the Identification and Reconciliation Engine (IRE)?
options: To match incoming data to existing CIs and decide which source may update each attribute
To build and refresh application service maps from traffic-based discovery data
To calculate the completeness, compliance, and correctness scores for each CI class
To schedule Discovery runs and decide which MID Server executes each probe
questions.explanation:
IRE applies identification rules to find existing CIs before inserting new ones, and reconciliation rules to decide which data source is authoritative for which attributes. Its job is CMDB integrity.

Scheduling, scoring, and mapping are handled by other components.

questions.stem: A hardware class identification rule has two identifier entries: serial number (priority 100) and name (priority 200). An incoming payload has a name but no serial number. What happens?
options: The payload is rejected because the highest-priority identifier entry cannot be evaluated
IRE evaluates the serial number entry with a null value, which matches every CI in the class
IRE always inserts a new CI whenever the highest-priority identifier attributes are missing
IRE skips the serial number entry because its attributes are empty and tries the name entry
questions.explanation:
Identifier entries are evaluated in priority order (lower number first). When the payload lacks values for an entry's criterion attributes, that entry is skipped and the next one is tried.

Rejecting or blindly inserting would defeat identification, and null values are not matched.

questions.stem: Why must a dependent CI, such as an application server instance, be sent to IRE with its relationship to a host?
options: Dependent CIs are identified in the context of the CI they depend on
Relationships are only needed so the dependent CI appears correctly in reports and dashboards
IRE ignores relationships entirely, so they can be added later with a separate import job
Dependent CIs cannot be stored in the CMDB unless their host CI was created manually first
questions.explanation:
A Tomcat instance named "default" could exist on hundreds of servers. Dependent CIs are identified within the scope of the CI they depend on, so without the relationship the payload can't be identified correctly.

Relationships are core to identification here, not just reporting.

questions.stem: Discovery and an SCCM integration both update a server's RAM. Discovery should win. What should you configure?
options: A reconciliation rule that gives Discovery priority for that attribute on the class
An identification rule that matches the server on serial number before name
A health inclusion rule that excludes SCCM-reported servers from correctness checks
A Data Manager policy that retires any server whose RAM value is changed by SCCM
questions.explanation:
Reconciliation rules define which discovery source is authoritative for which attributes, so a lower-priority source cannot overwrite data from a higher-priority one.

Identification decides which CI a payload matches. Health inclusion and Data Manager govern scoring and lifecycle.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of dynamic reconciliation rules?
options: To merge duplicate CIs automatically when two sources report the same device
To schedule CMDB Health jobs after each integration finishes loading its data
To delete any CI whose attribute values two or more sources disagree about
To resolve conflicting values, such as by last reported
questions.explanation:
Dynamic reconciliation resolves conflicting values among sources by strategy — last reported, most reported, largest, smallest — when static priority rules don't apply.

Deletion and merging are remediation actions; scheduling is unrelated.

questions.stem: What does Multisource CMDB provide?
options: The values each source reported for a CI, so conflicts can be seen and values recomputed
A replicated copy of the CMDB kept in a second instance for disaster recovery
A supported way for trusted integrations to write to the CMDB without going through IRE
Automatic deletion of CIs that only one data source has ever reported
questions.explanation:
Multisource CMDB keeps per-source reported values, letting you see what each source said about a CI, investigate conflicts, and recompute values from the stored source data. It works with IRE.

It is not replication, doesn't delete single-source CIs, and doesn't bypass IRE.

questions.stem: When are lookup rules used in identification?
options: When identifying values live on a related table
When calculating whether a CI has gone stale based on related records' update times
When choosing which MID Server should run discovery for a particular IP range
When building reports that join CI attributes from several related lookup tables
questions.explanation:
Lookup rules let IRE identify a CI using values stored in related lookup tables — for example, the serial number table or network adapters — which helps when a device has several identifiers.

They have no role in reporting, scheduling, or staleness.

questions.stem: Which component executes horizontal discovery probes and patterns inside the customer network?
options: The CMDB Health dashboard
The MID Server
The user's browser
The instance's scheduled job processor
questions.explanation:
The MID Server runs inside the network, executes probes and patterns against targets, and returns results to the instance. Discovery depends on it to reach on-premises infrastructure.

The instance orchestrates but cannot reach private networks directly.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of the horizontal discovery phases?
options: Identification, scanning, classification, exploration
Scanning, classification, identification, exploration
Classification, scanning, exploration, identification
Exploration, identification, classification, scanning
questions.explanation:
Discovery scans for open ports, classifies the device type, identifies whether it already exists in the CMDB, then explores it for detailed attributes and relationships.

Identification must follow classification because rules are class-specific.

questions.stem: What is a primary advantage of a Service Graph Connector over a custom import?
options: It's a certified integration that loads mapped data through IRE
It writes directly to CMDB tables, which avoids the overhead of identification
It only works with data produced by ServiceNow Discovery and its MID Servers
It removes the need for reconciliation rules because its data is always authoritative
questions.explanation:
Service Graph Connectors are certified integrations for sources such as Microsoft SCCM, Intune, and cloud providers. They use standard mappings and IRE, which gives you consistent, deduplicated data with far less effort than building your own import.

Reconciliation rules still determine which source wins.

questions.stem: An integrator wants a guided way to map a new third-party source to CMDB classes and load it through IRE without writing transform scripts. Which tool fits?
options: A legacy transform map that writes directly to cmdb_ci_server
CMDB Query Builder
IntegrationHub ETL
Flow Designer approval actions
questions.explanation:
IntegrationHub ETL provides a guided UI to map source data to CMDB classes and relationships and sends it through IRE, which is also how Service Graph Connectors are built.

Direct transform maps bypass IRE. Approvals and Query Builder are unrelated.

questions.stem: A team imports servers with a transform map that writes directly to cmdb_ci_server. Duplicates keep appearing. What is the root cause?
options: The MID Server used by the import is down, so records are inserted twice
CMDB Health jobs are disabled, so duplicate detection never runs for the class
The import bypasses IRE, so identification rules are never applied to the data
The servers are stale, and stale CIs are recreated each time they are imported
questions.explanation:
Writing directly to CMDB tables skips identification, so existing CIs aren't matched and duplicates are inserted. Route imports through IRE — with IntegrationHub ETL or IRE-aware transform logic — instead.

MID Server status, health jobs, and staleness don't create duplicates.

questions.stem: A custom scripted integration must create and update CIs correctly. How should it write to the CMDB?
options: By importing a CSV file directly into the cmdb_ci base table
By opening and editing each CI through the standard form UI
With GlideRecord inserts directly on each CMDB class table
Through the IRE API, so payloads are identified
questions.explanation:
Calling the IRE API (for example, the identification engine's create-or-update method) applies identification and reconciliation. Direct GlideRecord inserts and CSV loads bypass both.

Manual UI edits don't scale for an integration.

questions.stem: A new integration needs its own precedence in reconciliation rules. What must it have?
options: A Data Manager policy that retires CIs the integration hasn't updated recently
Its own discovery source value, so IRE can tell its data apart from other sources
Its own CI class, so its data never conflicts with what other sources report
Admin access to every CMDB table so it can overwrite values from other sources
questions.explanation:
Reconciliation rules are defined per discovery source. A new integration should register its own discovery source value so its data can be prioritized appropriately.

Broad admin access, new classes, and lifecycle policies don't establish precedence.

questions.stem: Why is manual CI creation discouraged for classes that have automated sources?
options: The platform blocks manual CI creation for any class that has a discovery pattern
Manual data isn't refreshed, can conflict with automated data, and tends to go stale
Manually created CIs cannot have relationships to discovered CIs in the CMDB
Manually created CIs are excluded from all reports, dashboards, and health scores
questions.explanation:
Manual records lack an automated source to keep them current and can collide with discovered data. Manual entry is appropriate for things no tool can discover, such as some logical CIs, with clear ownership.

Manual creation is possible, and manual CIs can have relationships and appear in reports.

questions.stem: What is the difference between horizontal discovery and top-down discovery?
options: They are identical processes that use different names in different releases of the platform
Horizontal inventories infrastructure; top-down maps one application service
Horizontal discovery only finds cloud resources, while top-down discovery finds on-premises servers
Top-down discovery doesn't use MID Servers, while horizontal discovery always requires one
questions.explanation:
Horizontal discovery builds broad infrastructure inventory. Top-down discovery follows the traffic from an entry point, such as a URL, to map the components of a specific application service.

Both use MID Servers, and horizontal discovery covers more than cloud.

questions.stem: Which table tracks which source reported a CI along with that source's native key?
options: cmdb_rel_ci
cmdb_health_result
sys_object_source
sys_user
questions.explanation:
sys_object_source records the source name, the native identifier from that source, and when it last reported, linking source data to the CI. It's useful for troubleshooting integrations.

cmdb_rel_ci holds relationships; the others are unrelated.

questions.stem: Select two benefits of routing every CI-writing integration through IRE. (Choose two.)
options: Duplicates are prevented by applying identification rules
Health scores no longer need to be calculated
Integrations run without any access control
Reconciliation rules prevent lower-priority sources from overwriting authoritative data
questions.explanation: IRE delivers both identification and reconciliation. Access control and health scoring are unaffected.

questions.stem: What are the three KPIs of CMDB Health?
options: Accuracy, timeliness, and cost
Discovery, identification, and reconciliation
Availability, performance, and capacity
Completeness, compliance, and correctness
questions.explanation:
CMDB Health scores completeness (required and recommended fields), compliance (against audits and desired state), and correctness (duplicates, orphans, and staleness).

The other sets describe operations metrics or ingestion steps.

questions.stem: Which metrics make up the completeness KPI?
options: Discovery schedule success
Audit results
Required and recommended fields
Duplicates and orphans
questions.explanation: Completeness measures whether required and recommended attributes are populated. Duplicates and orphans fall under correctness, and audits under compliance.

questions.stem: Select two metrics that count toward the correctness KPI. (Choose two.)
options: Missing required fields
Failed audits
Orphan CIs
Duplicate CIs
questions.explanation: Correctness covers duplicates, orphans, and stale CIs. Missing fields affect completeness, and failed audits affect compliance.

questions.stem: How is the compliance KPI measured?
options: By comparing CIs against audits that define desired attribute values or states
By counting the duplicate and orphan CIs found in each class during health jobs
By measuring how long each Discovery schedule takes to finish its scans
By counting how many users with the itil role have viewed each CI recently
questions.explanation:
Compliance audits check CIs against defined expectations — for example, that every production server has a managed-by group or specific configuration values. Failing CIs reduce the score.

Duplicates belong to correctness.

questions.stem: What makes a CI stale?
options: It has more relationships than the orphan rules for its class allow
It has no owner or managed-by group populated on its CI record
No source has updated it within its class's staleness period
It was created manually instead of by Discovery or an integration
questions.explanation:
Staleness measures how recently a CI was updated. If no source updates it within the configured period (60 days by default), it's flagged as stale, which suggests it may no longer exist.

Ownership, relationships, and creation method are measured differently.

questions.stem: What is an orphan CI?
options: A CI missing a relationship its orphan rule requires
A CI that two different sources update, with neither designated as authoritative
A CI that has no owner, managed-by group, or support group populated on its record
A CI that has been retired but still has open incidents or changes referencing it
questions.explanation:
Orphan rules define relationships a class should have. CIs without them are orphans — often a sign of incomplete discovery or leftover records.

Missing owners and multiple sources are separate concerns. Retired CIs are a lifecycle state.

questions.stem: A CMDB manager wants health scores to include only operational CIs and exclude retired ones. What should be configured?
options: Health inclusion rules for the classes
Principal class settings for the classes
Reconciliation rules for the classes
Identification rules for the classes
questions.explanation:
Health inclusion rules limit which CIs are evaluated, so retired or out-of-scope records don't distort scores.

Reconciliation and identification are IRE settings. Principal classes affect CI selection in forms.

questions.stem: IRE finds multiple existing CIs that match an incoming payload. What does it do?
options: It silently deletes all but the most recently updated CI before applying the payload
It creates a de-duplication task so the duplicates can be reviewed and remediated
It discards the payload permanently and blocks the source from sending that CI again
It merges the matching CIs automatically into one record without any review
questions.explanation:
When identification finds duplicates, IRE flags them and creates de-duplication tasks so someone can choose the main CI and remediate safely.

Silent deletion or automatic merging could lose data.

questions.stem: What happens when a duplicate is remediated with the duplicate CI remediation process?
options: A main CI is chosen and attributes, relationships, and related records move to it first
Both the main CI and its duplicates are deleted, and Discovery recreates the device later
The newest CI is always kept, and older duplicates are deleted without any review
Only the CI names are merged; relationships and related records stay on the duplicates
questions.explanation:
Remediation lets you pick the surviving CI and decide what to carry over — attributes, relationships, and related records such as incidents — before handling the duplicates.

Deleting both or keeping one blindly loses information.

questions.stem: Duplicates reappear every week after being remediated. What should you investigate first?
options: The identification rules, and whether the integration uses IRE
The number of CMDB groups defined for the class and whether any of them overlap
The principal class list and whether the duplicated class is included in it
The theme and color settings of the CMDB Health dashboard used to report duplicates
questions.explanation:
Recurring duplicates point to a root cause upstream: weak identification rules, payloads missing identifying attributes, or an integration bypassing IRE. Remediation alone treats the symptom.

The other items don't cause duplicates.

questions.stem: What is CMDB Data Manager used for?
options: Writing the identification rules IRE uses to match incoming payloads to CIs
Defining policies that retire, archive, and delete CIs, with tasks and approvals
Building and maintaining application service maps from discovered relationships
Running and scheduling horizontal Discovery against the organization's IP ranges
questions.explanation:
Data Manager provides governed lifecycle policies so CIs are retired, archived, and eventually deleted consistently, with tasks and approvals where needed.

Service maps, Discovery, and identification are elsewhere.

questions.stem: In what order should Data Manager lifecycle policies typically act on an outdated CI?
options: Archive, delete, retire
Delete, archive, retire
Retire, archive, delete
Delete only
questions.explanation:
A CI is first retired (taken out of service), then archived (moved out of active tables while preserved), and finally deleted when retention allows. That sequence preserves history.

Deleting first destroys records that may still be referenced.

questions.stem: What are principal classes used for?
options: Deciding which data source is authoritative for each attribute on a class
Filtering CI reference fields on task forms to the classes users most need
Calculating how many days a CI can go without updates before it is stale
Storing CIs that have been retired so they no longer appear in active lists
questions.explanation:
Principal classes are the classes users typically need to select — business applications, servers, services — and filtering by them keeps CI pickers on incident and change forms usable.

They don't affect reconciliation, staleness, or retirement.

questions.stem: Which experience gives CMDB managers a central place for health, search, and governance tasks?
options: Service Portal
CMDB Workspace
Discovery Admin console only
Employee Center
questions.explanation:
CMDB Workspace brings CMDB search, health, governance tasks, and insights together for CMDB managers and data stewards.

The portals target end users, and the Discovery console covers ingestion only.

questions.stem: A team needs to certify a specific set of CIs owned by one department. What helps define that set?
options: A reconciliation rule scoped to the department's sources
A CMDB group defined by a query or a manual list of CIs
A new CI class created just for that department's CIs
A Discovery schedule limited to the department's subnets
questions.explanation:
CMDB groups define sets of CIs for health, certification, and reporting — either by query or by listing them manually.

Creating classes for scoping, or using IRE and Discovery settings, would be misuse.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of data certification in CMDB governance?
options: Approving Discovery schedules before they run against production networks
Encrypting sensitive CI attributes so only certified users can read them
Having owners periodically verify that CI attribute values are accurate
Certifying the CMDB itself against ISO 27001 for external auditors
questions.explanation:
Certification policies send tasks to CI owners to confirm or correct attribute values, which is valuable for data no tool can discover.

It isn't an ISO certification, scheduling, or encryption feature.

questions.stem: Which CI attribute assignment best supports operational accountability for data quality?
options: The discovery source field, showing its origin
The CI's sys_id, used as its permanent key
The user recorded in the CI's created-by field
A managed-by group populated on every in-scope CI
questions.explanation:
The managed-by group (with owned-by and supported-by under CSDM) identifies who is responsible for the CI, which is what governance tasks and remediation need.

Created-by and sys_id don't express responsibility. Discovery source indicates origin, not ownership.

questions.stem: Under current CSDM guidance, which fields should be used to represent where a CI is in its lifecycle?
options: The updated-on timestamp of the CI
Only the legacy Install Status field value
Life Cycle Stage and Life Cycle Stage Status
The CI's short description field
questions.explanation:
CSDM standardizes lifecycle on Life Cycle Stage and Life Cycle Stage Status, which replace inconsistent use of install and operational status across classes.

Descriptions and timestamps aren't lifecycle fields.

questions.stem: A large number of servers are flagged as stale. What is the recommended handling?
options: Find out why sources stopped reporting, then retire confirmed decommissioned CIs via policy
Delete every stale CI immediately so the correctness score recovers before the next review
Turn off the staleness metric for the server class until the integrations are repaired
Run a script that updates each stale CI's timestamp so it no longer counts as stale
questions.explanation:
Staleness can mean decommissioned assets or a broken integration. Investigate first, then use governed lifecycle policies to retire confirmed decommissioned CIs.

Immediate deletion, disabling the metric, or faking updates all hide the real problem.

questions.stem: A class's health score suddenly drops after a new integration starts sending data. What is the most likely explanation?
options: More users have logged in to the CMDB Workspace since the integration went live
The health dashboard's theme was changed, which resets the class's scoring weights
The integration is creating CIs without required fields or creating duplicates
The principal class list was updated, which changes how health scores are weighted
questions.explanation:
New sources commonly introduce incomplete records or duplicates, which lower completeness and correctness. Check the integration's mappings and identification.

The other changes don't affect scores.

questions.stem: Why should health scores be tracked over time rather than checked once?
options: The platform doesn't support viewing a single score without historical data
Scores never change after the first calculation, so one check is only a formality
Tracking scores over time is a prerequisite for Discovery schedules to run
Trends show whether data quality is improving and expose regressions after changes
questions.explanation:
Trending shows the effect of remediation and catches regressions early. A single snapshot can't show whether the program is working.

Scores change continuously, and trending isn't a Discovery dependency.

questions.stem: What does CMDB Query Builder let you do that a standard list view cannot?
options: Edit attribute values on many CIs at once from a single list of results
Start a Discovery run against the CIs that match a saved list filter
Query across CI classes and related tables by following their relationships
Create or modify the identification rules used by IRE for a class
questions.explanation:
Query Builder queries across classes and relationships — for example, all databases supporting a business application through several hops. List views filter one table.

Bulk editing, Discovery, and identification are elsewhere.

questions.stem: A change manager needs every Linux server supporting a particular business application, including those connected through intermediate CIs. Which tool fits best?
options: A Data Manager policy
The server list view filtered by name
CMDB Query Builder
An identification rule
questions.explanation:
Relationship-based queries across classes are Query Builder's purpose. A server list can't follow relationships to the application.

Data Manager and identification rules aren't query tools.

questions.stem: What is Unified Map used for?
options: Visualizing CIs, their relationships, and service maps in one interactive map
Merging duplicate CIs after a de-duplication task has been approved
Scheduling Discovery runs and assigning MID Servers to each IP range
Calculating completeness, compliance, and correctness scores for each class
questions.explanation:
Unified Map provides one interactive visualization of CI relationships and service maps, with filtering and drill-down for impact analysis and troubleshooting.

It doesn't schedule, score, or remediate.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the CMDB and CSDM foundation dashboards?
options: To show whether foundational data is in place and where gaps are
To store attachments and evidence for CMDB certification tasks
To start Discovery runs and monitor their progress across MID Servers
To route normal and emergency changes to the right approvers
questions.explanation:
Foundation dashboards show the readiness of CMDB and CSDM data — whether foundation records, business applications, services, and their relationships exist and are populated — so teams can prioritize.

They aren't operational tools.

questions.stem: How does an accurate CMDB reduce mean time to resolve incidents?
options: Incidents linked to healthy CIs are closed automatically once monitoring clears the alert
Responders see affected CIs, dependencies, and recent changes, speeding diagnosis and routing
Alerts are suppressed for CIs with high health scores, which reduces incident volume
Support groups are no longer needed because the CMDB assigns incidents to individuals
questions.explanation:
Knowing what a CI supports, what it depends on, and what recently changed is how CMDB data shortens triage. Accurate support groups also improve routing.

The CMDB doesn't close incidents or remove the need for support teams.

questions.stem: How does CMDB data improve change management?
options: It approves standard and normal changes automatically when the CI is healthy
It replaces the change advisory board for changes to discovered CIs
It prevents any change from being scheduled against servers in production
It supports impact analysis by identifying affected services and dependent CIs
questions.explanation:
Change impact relies on relationships: which services and CIs a change touches. Better data means better risk assessment and fewer surprise outages.

Automated approvals and CAB replacement aren't CMDB functions.

questions.stem: Select two business outcomes most directly enabled by a trusted CMDB. (Choose two.)
options: Elimination of all outages
More accurate change impact assessment
Removal of the need for asset management
Faster incident triage through dependency context
questions.explanation: Dependency context and impact analysis are direct outcomes of reliable data. No CMDB eliminates outages, and asset management remains a separate discipline.

questions.stem: An executive asks whether CMDB governance investment is paying off. What evidence is most persuasive?
options: The overall size of the CMDB database in gigabytes compared with the previous year
The total number of CI classes created or extended since the governance program started
The number of users who have been granted access to the CMDB Workspace this year
Health score trends shown alongside metrics such as change success rate and resolution time
questions.explanation: Improving data quality tied to better operational outcomes demonstrates value. Class counts, user counts, and data volume say nothing about quality or impact.

questions.stem: How can CMDB Query Builder results be reused beyond the builder itself?
options: Each query requires a fresh Discovery run before its results can be reused
Saved queries can be used as a source for reports and scheduled exports
Saved queries are deleted automatically after each run to protect performance
Results can only be viewed once and must be rebuilt for every new session
questions.explanation: Saving queries lets you reuse them in reporting and schedule them, so complex relationship queries become ongoing insight rather than one-off searches.

questions.stem: A health dashboard shows low completeness for the server class. What is the most useful next step?
options: Drill into failing CIs and missing fields to find patterns
Disable completeness scoring for the server class until the integrations are reviewed
Export the dashboard to PDF, attach it to a task, and close the task as reviewed
Delete the server class and recreate it so the scores reset with a clean baseline
questions.explanation:
Drill-down shows which attributes and sources cause the gap, so fixes can target the root cause, often an integration mapping.

Disabling or deleting hides the problem.

questions.stem: Why use a relationship-aware view rather than a flat list when assessing what an outage on a database server affects?
options: Impact depends on what relies on the server, which relationships show
Flat lists take much longer to load than relationship views when CMDB classes are large
Flat lists cannot be filtered by environment, location, or support group
Relationship views can display more attribute columns than a standard flat list
questions.explanation: What an outage affects is defined by dependencies. A list of servers can't show which applications and services sit on top of them.

questions.stem: Which statement about CMDB insight tools is true?
options: They correct bad data automatically whenever a user views an inaccurate CI
They replace the need for CSDM because they infer service models from CI data
They only work with data that came from ServiceNow Discovery, not integrations
Their value depends on the quality of the underlying CMDB data
questions.explanation:
Maps, queries, and dashboards are only as accurate as the CMDB. Governance makes insight trustworthy.

Insight tools don't fix data, work with any well-identified source, and don't replace a data model.

questions.stem: What is the Common Service Data Model (CSDM)?
options: A prescriptive framework for modeling services and applications in the CMDB
A library of Discovery patterns for identifying common applications and infrastructure
A reporting plugin that adds service dashboards to the CMDB Workspace
A licensing model that determines which CMDB classes an organization can use
questions.explanation:
CSDM standardizes where and how to model business and technical services, applications, and their relationships, so products across the platform share consistent data.

It isn't a discovery tool, license, or plugin.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a business application and an application service in CSDM?
options: Business applications only exist in the asset table and cannot be related to CIs
A business application is the software; an application service is a deployed instance
They are the same record, labeled differently depending on which team is viewing it
An application service is a desktop application; a business application is a web application
questions.explanation:
A business application ("Payroll") is a logical portfolio record. Application services ("Payroll – Production") are deployed instances that relate to the infrastructure CIs delivering them.

Confusing the two is the most common CSDM modeling error.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a business service from a technical service?
options: Business services serve business users; technical services support IT
Technical services cannot have service offerings, while business services always do
Business services are always offered to external customers; technical services are internal
There is no difference; the terms describe the same record type in different releases
questions.explanation:
Business services are what the business consumes, such as email or HR self-service. Technical services, such as database hosting, are IT capabilities that support them.

Both can have offerings.

questions.stem: Why does CSDM recommend service offerings?
options: They store the hardware and software attributes of the CIs that deliver the service
They are used only for chargeback, to bill business units for the services they consume
They replace business applications as the portfolio record for each piece of software
They define a service's specific commitments, such as SLAs, support groups, and availability
questions.explanation:
Offerings carry the commitments: SLAs, support and approval groups, and availability. They're what tasks and requests reference.

They complement rather than replace other records.

questions.stem: What is the recommended starting point when adopting CSDM?
options: Establish foundation data, then applications and services, in stages
Customize all CSDM tables to match the current org chart before loading data
Skip foundation data and begin with technical services, which have no dependencies
Model every service offering in detail before loading any foundation data
questions.explanation:
CSDM adoption is staged (crawl, walk, run, fly), starting with foundation data such as companies, locations, and groups, then business applications and application services.

Starting at the end or customizing first leads to rework.

questions.stem: In CSDM, which domain does the business application record belong to?
options: Service consumption
Foundation
Build and integration
Design and planning
questions.explanation:
Business applications are portfolio records in the design and planning domain (called the "Design" domain in earlier CSDM versions). Consumption covers business services and offerings; foundation covers reference data such as companies and locations.

Domain names changed between CSDM versions, so confirm against the version your instance follows.

questions.stem: How should a business service offering connect to the infrastructure that delivers it under CSDM?
options: It should not be connected, since offerings describe commitments, not infrastructure
Through the application service that delivers it, which relates to the infrastructure CIs
Through a text field on the offering that lists the names of the servers
Directly to every server involved, bypassing application services and offerings entirely
questions.explanation:
The service-to-infrastructure path runs through application services, which hold the dependency on infrastructure. That path is what makes impact analysis work.

Direct links to servers bypass the model, and text fields aren't relationships.

questions.stem: A new class extends cmdb_ci_server. What does it get from its parent?
options: The parent's attributes and, unless overridden, its identification rules
Nothing until an administrator copies the parent's dictionary entries by hand
The parent's CI records, which are copied into the new class automatically
Only the parent's name; every attribute has to be recreated on the new class
questions.explanation:
Class extension is inheritance: child classes get the parent's attributes and, unless they define their own, its identification and reconciliation rules.

No attributes need recreating, and existing records stay in their own class.

questions.stem: Why is "name" alone usually a weak identifier for hardware CIs?
options: Names only exist on CIs that were created manually
Names are encrypted, so IRE can't compare them
Name fields can't be used in identification rules at all
Names aren't guaranteed unique and change often
questions.explanation:
Hostnames are reused, renamed, and duplicated across environments. Strong identifiers such as serial numbers are stable and unique, so name is usually a lower-priority fallback.

Name can be used in rules, isn't encrypted, and exists on discovered CIs too.

questions.stem: A child class has no identification rule of its own. How does IRE identify its CIs?
options: It rejects every payload for that class with an error
It inserts a new CI every time because there's no rule
It uses the rule of whichever class was created most recently
It uses the nearest parent class's identification rule
questions.explanation:
Identification rules are inherited. Without its own rule, a class uses its nearest ancestor's rule, which is why most hardware classes share the hardware rule.

IRE doesn't blindly insert, reject everything, or pick an unrelated rule.

questions.stem: An integration updates the same CIs every five minutes, overwriting values that another source updates daily. Which reconciliation feature limits how often a source may update a CI?
options: Orphan rules
Principal class settings
Health inclusion rules
Data refresh rules
questions.explanation:
Data refresh rules set how much time must pass before a source is allowed to update a CI again, which reduces churn from noisy sources.

Inclusion, orphan, and principal class settings govern health scoring and form filtering.

questions.stem: At what level are reconciliation rules defined?
options: Per user, based on the roles of the user running the import
Once for the entire CMDB, applying to every class in the same way
Per CI record, set individually by each CI's owner
Per class and attribute, inherited by child classes unless overridden
questions.explanation:
Reconciliation rules name a class, the attributes they govern, and the source priority, and child classes inherit them. That granularity lets Discovery own technical attributes while an asset tool owns financial ones.

A single global rule is too coarse, and per-record or per-user rules would be unmanageable.

questions.stem: Which relationship type best describes an application that runs on a server?
options: Contains::Contained by
Sends data to::Receives data from
Members::Member of
Runs on::Runs
questions.explanation:
"Runs on::Runs" is the standard type for software running on a host. Contains is for containment, Members for clusters and groups, and Sends data to for data flows.

Using consistent relationship types keeps maps and impact analysis accurate.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of suggested relationships in CI Class Manager?
options: To delete relationships that don't match the class definition
To guide which relationship types are expected between classes
To replace identification rules for dependent CIs
To create relationships automatically for every CI in the class
questions.explanation:
Suggested relationships define the relationships that make sense for a class, guiding users and integrations toward consistent modeling.

They don't create or delete relationships on their own, and they don't replace identification.

questions.stem: How do containment and hosting rules support identification?
options: They define how long retired CIs are contained in archive tables
They define which users are allowed to contain and host new CI classes
They define valid paths for dependent CIs, like a VM hosted on a hypervisor
They define which MID Server hosts each Discovery schedule in the network
questions.explanation:
Containment and hosting rules describe how dependent CIs relate to the CIs they live in or on, which IRE uses when identifying them in context.

MID Server assignment, user permissions, and archiving are unrelated.

questions.stem: Where are a class's recommended fields defined, which feed the completeness KPI?
options: In the Discovery schedule that populates the class
In the CMDB Health dashboard's color settings
In each user's personal list layout for the class
In CI Class Manager
questions.explanation:
Class Manager lets you mark attributes as recommended, and completeness scoring checks whether CIs populate them.

List layouts, Discovery schedules, and dashboard colors don't define data expectations.

questions.stem: What does an IRE payload contain?
options: Only the sys_id of each CI to update, with no attributes included
A list of users who should own each CI after it is created
A SQL statement that IRE runs against the CMDB tables directly
CI items with class and attributes, plus relationships
questions.explanation:
IRE takes structured items (class name and values) and relations, then identifies, reconciles, and writes them. Sending relationships lets dependent CIs be identified.

Sending only sys_ids skips identification, and IRE never runs raw SQL.

questions.stem: In a reconciliation rule, how is source precedence expressed?
options: By whichever source has sent the most records
By a priority number, where a lower number means higher priority
By the order sources were installed, where the oldest always wins
By the alphabetical order of the source names
questions.explanation:
Each source gets a priority, and lower numbers win for the attributes the rule covers. That makes precedence explicit and adjustable.

Installation order, names, and volume don't determine precedence.

questions.stem: A server's RAM value keeps changing, and nobody knows which source is changing it. Where should you look?
options: The CI's short description history
The list of principal classes
The CMDB Health dashboard's overall score
The multisource view (CMDB 360) for that CI
questions.explanation:
The multisource view shows the value each source reported and when, which identifies the conflicting source quickly.

Descriptions, overall scores, and principal classes don't show per-source values.

questions.stem: A payload lacks values for every identifier entry in its class's identification rule. What happens?
options: IRE returns an error instead of risking a duplicate
IRE stores the payload and retries identification every hour indefinitely
IRE inserts a new CI anyway, using the name as a temporary identifier
IRE updates the most recently created CI in the class with the payload
questions.explanation:
Without identifying values, IRE can't safely decide whether the CI exists, so it reports an error rather than guessing. Fixing the source payload is the remedy.

Guessing would create duplicates or corrupt unrelated CIs.

questions.stem: Which attribute is typically the strongest identifier for physical hardware?
options: Serial number
Hostname
Assigned user
IP address
questions.explanation: Serial numbers are assigned by the manufacturer and rarely change, so they're the preferred hardware identifier. Hostnames get renamed, IPs get reassigned, and assigned users change all the time.

questions.stem: A company has several segmented networks that can't reach each other. How should MID Servers be deployed for Discovery?
options: Place MID Servers where they can reach the targets in each segment
Skip MID Servers and let the instance connect to targets directly
Use one MID Server in the DMZ to reach every network over the internet
Install a MID Server on each laptop that should be discovered
questions.explanation:
MID Servers need network access to the devices they discover, so segmented networks typically need MID Servers in or near each segment.

Routing all discovery through one DMZ host or the internet is unsafe, laptops aren't MID hosts, and the instance can't reach private networks directly.

questions.stem: Where does Discovery get the credentials it uses to log in to targets?
options: Discovery doesn't need credentials for any kind of exploration
From credentials stored on the instance, used by the MID Server
From the discovery admin's personal account, used for every probe
From each target device, which sends its password to the instance on request
questions.explanation:
Credentials are stored securely on the instance and used by MID Servers to authenticate. Credential affinity remembers which credential worked for which target.

Devices don't volunteer passwords, personal accounts are a security risk, and deep exploration needs credentials.

questions.stem: A team wants to find out which devices are alive on a range without exploring them in detail. What should they run?
options: A full configuration item discovery
An IP-scan-only discovery schedule
A CMDB Health correctness job
A Service Mapping top-down discovery
questions.explanation:
IP scan schedules find responsive devices and open ports without classifying or exploring them — useful for coverage checks.

Full discovery goes much deeper, Service Mapping starts from an application, and health jobs don't scan networks.

questions.stem: What do Discovery patterns do?
options: They define how to identify and explore a type of CI
They define the health scoring weights used for each class
They define which users can run Discovery schedules on the instance
They define the visual layout of the Unified Map for each class
questions.explanation:
Patterns are the instructions Discovery follows to collect attributes and relationships for a type of CI, and they can be extended with the pattern designer.

Map layout, permissions, and health weights are configured elsewhere.

questions.stem: A Discovery schedule should skip a range of sensitive industrial devices. What should be configured?
options: A health inclusion rule that ignores the devices' CIs
A Data Manager policy that retires the devices after discovery
An exclusion for that range in the schedule's IP configuration
A reconciliation rule that gives the devices lowest priority
questions.explanation:
Excluding addresses from the schedule keeps Discovery from probing them at all.

Health inclusion, reconciliation, and Data Manager act after data exists — they don't stop probes.

questions.stem: How does ServiceNow discover resources in public clouds such as AWS and Azure?
options: By installing a MID Server inside every virtual machine in the cloud
Through cloud discovery with a provider service account
By asking each cloud account owner to enter resources manually
Public cloud resources can't be discovered
questions.explanation:
Cloud discovery queries the provider's APIs with a configured service account, collecting resources such as VMs, databases, and networks. Service Graph Connectors are another option for some providers.

MIDs aren't installed in every VM, and manual entry doesn't scale.

questions.stem: Devices that are often off the corporate network, such as remote laptops, need regular inventory updates. What helps?
options: Asking users to update their laptop records each month
Agent-based collection, such as Agent Client Collector
More frequent agentless IP scans of the corporate ranges
Excluding remote laptops from the CMDB entirely
questions.explanation:
Agents report from the device wherever it is, which suits endpoints that agentless discovery can't reach reliably.

Scanning corporate ranges misses off-network devices, and manual updates or exclusion leave gaps.

questions.stem: How is a Service Graph Connector typically added to an instance?
options: Enabled by default on every instance with no configuration
Purchased from the third-party vendor and installed on the MID Server
Installed from the ServiceNow Store, then configured with its guided setup
Written from scratch by the customer as a scripted REST API
questions.explanation:
Connectors are Store applications with guided setup for credentials, scheduling, and options, which keeps deployment consistent.

They aren't custom-built, enabled by default, or installed on MID Servers as vendor software.

questions.stem: What data does a Service Graph Connector for an endpoint management tool such as Microsoft SCCM or Intune typically bring into the CMDB?
options: Computers, hardware details, and installed software
Users' email messages and calendar entries
Business applications and their portfolio owners
Business service offerings and their SLAs
questions.explanation:
Endpoint tools know about devices, hardware, and installed software, which is what their connectors load.

Portfolio data, service offerings, and email aren't endpoint management data.

questions.stem: Before running a new IntegrationHub ETL transform against production data, how can an implementer check what IRE will do?
options: ETL transforms can't be tested before they run
Ask IRE to email a summary of the changes it would make
Run it in production and fix any duplicates afterward
Use the ETL test run to preview and roll back
questions.explanation:
IntegrationHub ETL lets you test with sample data, review what IRE would insert or update, and roll back test results, which catches mapping mistakes early.

Testing in production is risky, and IRE doesn't email previews.

questions.stem: Which engine processes IntegrationHub ETL transformations before sending data to IRE?
options: The Robust Transform Engine
The Service Portal widget engine
The Performance Analytics engine
The Flow Designer approval engine
questions.explanation:
IntegrationHub ETL is built on the Robust Transform Engine (RTE), which transforms source data into the payloads IRE processes.

The other engines handle analytics, approvals, and portal rendering.

questions.stem: A legacy transform map must keep running, but it should go through IRE. What can be used in the transform script?
options: CMDBTransformUtil, to pass each row through IRE
A business rule that deletes duplicates after each import completes
A GlideRecord insert on cmdb_ci, to bypass the transform map entirely
A client script that blocks duplicate entries on the import form
questions.explanation:
CMDBTransformUtil lets a transform map hand records to IRE, so identification and reconciliation apply even for older imports.

Direct inserts bypass IRE, cleaning up afterward treats symptoms, and client scripts don't run during imports.

questions.stem: What is the role of the staging table in an import set?
options: It permanently stores the final CI records that users work with
It holds the list of users allowed to run the import
It holds raw imported data before it's transformed
It stores the health scores calculated for imported CIs
questions.explanation:
Import sets load raw data into a staging table, and transforms then map it to targets — ideally through IRE for CMDB data. Keeping raw data separate makes troubleshooting easier.

The final CIs live in CMDB tables, and staging tables don't store permissions or scores.

questions.stem: Two sources report the same manufacturer as "Hewlett Packard Enterprise" and "HPE". Why normalize these values during ingestion?
options: Consistent values make reporting and matching reliable
Normalization encrypts manufacturer data so only admins can read it
Normalization deletes CIs from manufacturers that aren't recognized
Normalized values are required before the MID Server can start
questions.explanation:
Normalizing manufacturer and model data, often through product models, makes counts, lifecycle reporting, and matching reliable.

It isn't encryption, a MID Server prerequisite, or a deletion mechanism.

questions.stem: What is the main benefit of delta imports over full imports for a large integration?
options: Delta imports don't need a schedule and run whenever data changes
Delta imports skip IRE entirely, so they can never create duplicates
Only changed records are processed, cutting load time and processing
Delta imports delete every CI that wasn't included in the latest file
questions.explanation:
Processing only what changed reduces load on the source and the instance and shortens run times. Periodic full loads can still catch drift.

Delta imports still go through IRE, don't delete unrelated CIs, and still run on schedules.

questions.stem: A Discovery run fails for a group of servers. Where should an administrator start troubleshooting?
options: The CMDB Health dashboard's completeness score for the server class
The discovery status, logs, and ECC queue for those devices
The principal class list, to confirm servers are included
The CSDM foundation dashboard for missing business applications
questions.explanation:
Discovery status, logs, and the ECC queue show what the MID Server tried and what came back — credential failures, unreachable ports, and pattern errors.

Health scores, principal classes, and CSDM dashboards don't show discovery errors.

questions.stem: When is manual creation the expected way to populate CMDB records?
options: For network devices, because Discovery can't classify switches or routers
For every server, because discovered server data is usually out of date
For logical records no tool can discover, such as business applications
Never; every CMDB record must be created by an integration or Discovery
questions.explanation:
Logical records such as business applications are defined by people. Even then, they need owners and governance to stay accurate.

Servers and network devices are discoverable, and some records can't come from tools at all.

questions.stem: How is a class's overall CMDB Health score derived?
options: From its three KPIs, combined by weight
From the age of the oldest CI in the class compared with the newest
From the number of Discovery schedules that target the class
From the number of users who opened CIs of the class during the week
questions.explanation:
The overall score combines the three KPIs using configurable weights, so organizations can emphasize what matters most to them.

Usage, CI age, and schedule counts aren't part of the health model.

questions.stem: What is the difference between required and recommended fields for completeness?
options: They're the same, and the platform uses the terms interchangeably
Required fields must be populated; recommended fields should be, and both count
Required fields are set by users; recommended fields are set by Discovery only
Recommended fields are mandatory on the form; required fields are optional
questions.explanation:
Required fields are must-haves, and recommended fields are expected for useful data. Completeness measures both, so gaps in either lower the score.

Who populates them doesn't define them, and the terms aren't interchangeable.

questions.stem: How does the duplicates metric identify duplicate CIs?
options: It compares every CI's short description with every other CI in the class
It counts CIs that were created on the same day by the same source
It counts CIs that share the same assigned-to user or support group
It counts CIs that IRE or remediation processes have flagged as duplicates
questions.explanation:
Duplicate detection comes from identification — IRE flags CIs that match the same identifiers — and the metric reports those flagged CIs.

Descriptions, assignments, and creation dates don't indicate duplication.

questions.stem: Network devices are discovered weekly, but some manually maintained classes are updated only twice a year. How should staleness be handled?
options: Set staleness rules per class to fit how each class is actually maintained
Delete manually maintained classes so they don't affect the score
Use the same short staleness period for every class to keep things simple
Turn off staleness for every class, since some classes are manual
questions.explanation:
Staleness periods are configurable per class. A period that fits discovered devices would wrongly flag manual classes, which are better covered by certification.

One-size-fits-all settings, disabling staleness, or deleting classes all hide real problems.

questions.stem: Where are orphan rules for a class typically configured?
options: In the user's personal notification preferences
In the Discovery schedule that populates the class
In each CI's form layout, using a UI policy
In CI Class Manager's health settings
questions.explanation:
Orphan rules live with the class's health configuration, defining which relationships a CI of that class should have.

Discovery schedules, UI policies, and notification preferences don't define data rules.

questions.stem: A compliance audit finds production servers without a managed-by group. What can the audit be configured to do?
options: Create remediation tasks for the failing CIs so owners can fix them
Assign the CIs to the CMDB administrator's group automatically
Lower the KPI's weight so the failure doesn't affect the overall score
Delete the failing CIs so they no longer lower the compliance score
questions.explanation:
Audits can generate remediation tasks for failures, turning a score into actionable work.

Deleting CIs, dumping them on admins, or reweighting the KPI all avoid fixing the data.

questions.stem: Remediation tasks for data quality issues need to reach the people who can fix them. What CI attribute is typically used to route them?
options: The discovery source
The CI's sys_class_name
The managed-by group
The created-by user
questions.explanation:
The managed-by group is accountable for maintaining the CI, so it's the natural routing target for data quality tasks.

Creators, sources, and class names don't identify responsibility.

questions.stem: Which CMDB Data Manager policy type asks owners to confirm that CIs still exist and are accurate?
options: Deletion
Attestation
Archive
Retirement
questions.explanation: Attestation policies send tasks to owners to confirm or update CIs. Retire, archive, and delete policies act on the CIs' lifecycle instead.

questions.stem: How do CMDB Data Manager policies determine which CIs they act on?
options: By acting only on CIs whose class is listed as a principal class
With filters or CMDB groups that select the target CIs
By acting on every CI in the CMDB at once each time it runs
By picking a random sample of CIs each time the policy runs
questions.explanation:
Policies scope their targets with conditions or CMDB groups — for example, "servers not discovered in 90 days".

Acting on everything or at random would be dangerous, and principal classes are about form filtering.

questions.stem: Why should a policy require approval before CIs are deleted?
options: To confirm CIs aren't still needed before removal
To slow the policy down so it doesn't use too much processing
Because deleted CIs must be emailed to the auditors first
Because the platform can't delete CIs without a manager's password
questions.explanation:
Approval gives owners a chance to catch mistakes — a CI may still be in use or referenced by open tasks — before data is lost.

Passwords, performance throttling, and emailing auditors aren't the reason.

questions.stem: An organization moving to CSDM lifecycle fields has CIs with legacy install status values. What should be done?
options: Delete every CI that uses legacy status values and rediscover them
Keep using install status and ignore the CSDM lifecycle fields
Map the legacy values to Life Cycle Stage and Life Cycle Stage Status
Copy install status into the CI's description field for reference
questions.explanation:
Mapping legacy statuses to the CSDM fields preserves meaning while standardizing on the new model.

Deleting CIs loses history, ignoring CSDM fragments the model, and descriptions aren't structured data.

questions.stem: Who is typically responsible for the definition and data quality of a specific CI class?
options: The external auditor
Every user with the itil role
The MID Server service account
The class owner
questions.explanation:
Class owners are accountable for how a class is defined and how good its data is, working with the CMDB manager and data stewards.

Broad user groups, auditors, and service accounts don't own data quality.

questions.stem: What is the benefit of documenting a RACI for each important CI class?
options: It lets the platform skip health calculations for the class
Everyone knows who maintains, approves, and uses the class's data
It replaces the need for identification rules on those classes
It removes the need for Discovery on documented classes
questions.explanation:
Clear roles — who's responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed — prevent data quality gaps from falling between teams.

Documentation doesn't replace identification, health calculations, or Discovery.

questions.stem: The same kind of duplicate keeps appearing — for example, VMs reported by two tools with different name formats. What helps remediate these at scale?
options: Remediating each duplicate by hand, with each person using their own approach
Increasing the staleness period for VMs so the duplicates age out of reports
De-duplication templates that define how to resolve that pattern consistently
Turning off identification for virtual machine classes until the tools agree
questions.explanation:
Templates capture how to resolve a recurring duplicate pattern — which CI to keep and what to merge — so remediation is consistent and faster. Fixing the identification root cause still matters.

Ad hoc fixes are slow, disabling identification causes more duplicates, and staleness doesn't affect duplication.

questions.stem: Besides keeping CI pickers usable, why do principal classes matter for data governance?
options: They are the only classes that can have health scores calculated
They prevent non-principal classes from being discovered at all
They are the only classes that IRE will identify and reconcile
They focus governance effort on the classes users actually work with
questions.explanation:
Principal classes are the ones most visible to users on tasks, so they're a sensible priority for governance.

Other classes still get health scores, identification, and discovery.

questions.stem: A class that's maintained manually shows many stale CIs, even though the data is accurate. What is a better way to keep that class trustworthy?
options: Exclude the class from every CMDB report and dashboard so it isn't counted
Use periodic certification by owners instead of relying on discovery updates
Write a script that updates every CI's timestamp each night so none look stale
Delete the class's stale CIs and recreate them from a spreadsheet every month
questions.explanation:
Certification asks owners to confirm data that no tool updates, which is the right control for manual classes. Staleness settings can be adjusted to match.

Faking updates, recreating CIs, or hiding the class all undermine trust.

questions.stem: Why should custom relationship types be avoided where a standard type fits?
options: Standard types keep maps and impact analysis consistent
Custom types are automatically deleted at each upgrade
Standard relationship types are the only ones IRE can store
Custom relationship types are blocked by the platform
questions.explanation:
Features and reports expect standard relationship types. Custom ones fragment the model and can break impact analysis.

Custom types are allowed and stored, and upgrades don't delete them — they're just harder to govern.

questions.stem: How are CMDB Health scorecard results usually presented to show where action is needed?
options: With thresholds that color scores by status, such as red, yellow, and green
As a single number for the whole company, with no class or KPI breakdown
Only in a spreadsheet export that is sent to CMDB managers once a year
As raw lists of every CI in each class, with no scoring or thresholds applied
questions.explanation:
Thresholds and color coding make it easy to see which classes and KPIs need attention, with drill-down to details.

A single number hides detail, raw lists lack context, and annual exports are too slow.

questions.stem: A decommissioned server still has old incidents and changes that reference it. What should happen to its CI?
options: Leave it operational so the old records stay valid
Retire it so its history stays intact
Rename it so nobody can find it in searches
Delete it at once so it no longer appears in any CI picker
questions.explanation:
Retiring keeps the CI and its history for reporting and audit while making clear it's no longer in service. Later archiving and deletion can follow policy.

Deleting breaks references, leaving it operational is inaccurate, and renaming obscures data.

questions.stem: Retired CIs accumulate for years and slow down queries. What does an archive policy do?
options: Deletes every retired CI immediately with no way to recover it
Marks retired CIs operational again so they're used in reports
Copies retired CIs into the knowledge base as articles
Moves retired CIs out of active tables, preserving them
questions.explanation:
Archiving removes old CIs from active tables, improving performance, while keeping them available for history and compliance. Deletion, if needed, comes later.

Immediate deletion loses data, reactivating is wrong, and knowledge articles aren't archives.

questions.stem: How is a certification policy typically set up?
options: With a CI filter, attributes to certify, and a schedule
With a Discovery pattern that certifies attributes during each scan
With a reconciliation rule that marks the owner's source as certified
With a principal class flag that certifies all CIs in the class
questions.explanation:
Certification policies define which CIs, which attributes, and how often owners must confirm them.

Patterns, reconciliation rules, and principal class flags don't certify data.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a compliance audit and a certification?
options: An audit checks CIs automatically; certification asks people
An audit is done only by external auditors; certification is done by Discovery
There's no difference; the platform uses both names for one feature
An audit deletes failing CIs; certification archives them
questions.explanation:
Audits are automated checks against defined expectations. Certification relies on owners verifying values that rules can't check.

Neither is reserved for external auditors, and neither deletes or archives CIs.

questions.stem: A team wants to add a new custom CI class. What should happen first?
options: A governance review of whether an existing class fits
Copy an existing class and rename all of its fields
Add a new table without extending cmdb_ci for flexibility
Create the class directly in production and announce it
questions.explanation:
Governance review prevents class sprawl. Often an existing class — or a CSDM-aligned one — already fits.

Creating classes ad hoc, outside the hierarchy, or by copying leads to inconsistent data.

questions.stem: Health inclusion rules already exclude retired servers. How do CMDB groups differ from them?
options: CMDB groups replace identification rules for the CIs they contain
CMDB groups define named sets of CIs for governance
CMDB groups decide which data source wins for each attribute
CMDB groups are the only way to exclude CIs from health scores
questions.explanation:
Inclusion rules decide what counts in health scoring. CMDB groups define reusable sets of CIs — for certification, Data Manager policies, reporting, and health views.

They don't replace identification or reconciliation.

questions.stem: Two discovery tools report the same servers with different serial number formats, creating duplicates. What is the best fix?
options: Delete duplicates by hand each week as they reappear
Normalize serial numbers or use lookup rules
Exclude servers from the CMDB Health correctness KPI
Turn off one of the tools permanently, even if it has unique data
questions.explanation:
Making identifying data consistent — by normalizing values or using lookup rules — lets IRE recognize the same server from both sources.

Turning off a source loses data, manual cleanup treats symptoms, and hiding the KPI hides the problem.

questions.stem: An application CI is flagged as an orphan because it has no host relationship. What are the reasonable remediations?
options: Add the missing relationship if the application is live, or retire it if not
Mark the application's class as a principal class so its orphans aren't checked
Delete the orphan rule so the application and others like it stop being flagged
Change the application's class to a class that doesn't have any orphan rule
questions.explanation:
An orphan either has a missing relationship that should be added or is no longer real and should be retired.

Removing the rule, abusing principal classes, or reclassifying the CI hides the problem.

questions.stem: Where should a CMDB team focus first when starting a health improvement program?
options: High-value classes used in key processes, like servers and business apps
The classes with the fewest CIs, because they're the quickest ones to fix
Classes that no process uses, since changes there carry no operational risk
Every class in the CMDB at once, giving each class exactly the same priority
questions.explanation:
Starting where data drives incident, change, and other key processes delivers visible value quickly.

Trying to fix everything at once stalls progress, and small or unused classes deliver little value.

questions.stem: Why use CMDB Data Manager policies instead of scheduled scripts to remove old CIs?
options: Policies give consistent, auditable lifecycle actions with approvals and tasks
Policies run faster than scripts because they bypass access controls entirely
Policies delete CIs immediately, without the delays of any review or approval
Scheduled scripts can't run against CMDB tables, so they can't remove any CIs
questions.explanation:
Policies make lifecycle actions governed: defined criteria, approvals, tasks, and a record of what happened. Scripts are easy to get wrong and hard to audit.

Scripts can run, policies respect access controls, and policies include review steps.

questions.stem: A class has completeness at 100%. Does that mean its data is accurate?
options: No, because completeness scores are always calculated lower than accuracy
Not necessarily — fields can be populated with wrong or outdated values
Yes, because complete data is by definition also accurate and up to date
Yes, because the platform validates the truth of every value before saving
questions.explanation:
Completeness checks that fields are filled, not that values are right. Correctness, audits, and certification address accuracy.

Populated doesn't mean correct, and the platform doesn't validate the truth of every value.

questions.stem: What can be done from the health dashboard when it shows failing CIs?
options: Change failing scores to passing directly on the dashboard
Nothing; the dashboard is display-only and can't lead to action
Delete all failing CIs in one step from the dashboard
Drill into them and create remediation tasks
questions.explanation:
The dashboard is a starting point for remediation, with drill-down and task creation that routes fixes to the right teams.

Mass deletion or overriding scores would undermine the program.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the goal of CMDB governance?
options: Ensure every CI is discovered by at least three different tools
Keep CMDB data trustworthy enough for the processes that depend on it
Load as many CIs into the CMDB as possible, whatever their quality
Lock down the CMDB so that only administrators can view it
questions.explanation:
Governance exists so incident, change, security, and other processes can rely on CMDB data. Quality and fitness for purpose matter more than volume.

Multiple sources and restricted visibility don't define the goal.

questions.stem: An analyst wants servers that have had more than five incidents this quarter. Can CMDB Query Builder help?
options: No, Query Builder can only query CI attributes on a single class
Yes, queries can include tables such as incidents
Yes, but only if each incident is converted into a CI first
No, incidents must be exported and joined in a spreadsheet
questions.explanation:
Query Builder can combine CMDB classes with related non-CMDB tables, such as tasks referencing CIs, which makes operational questions like this answerable.

It isn't limited to a single class, and no exports or conversions are needed.

questions.stem: In CMDB Query Builder, how do you find databases two relationship hops away from a business application?
options: Run a Discovery schedule scoped to the business application
Add the intermediate classes to the query and connect them with relationships
Ask the database owners to list which applications they support
Filter the database list by the business application's name in a text field
questions.explanation:
Query Builder models the path: application → application service or server → database, connected by relationships. That's what lets it traverse hops.

Text filters, surveys, and Discovery don't traverse relationships.

questions.stem: From a CI's record, a responder opens Unified Map. What can they do there?
options: Edit the identification rule that applies to the CI's class
Approve changes for every CI shown on the map
Expand relationships outward from the CI and see connected CIs
Run CMDB Health jobs for every CI on the map at once
questions.explanation:
Unified Map starts from a CI and expands its relationships, so responders can see what it depends on and what depends on it.

Identification rules, health jobs, and change approvals are handled elsewhere.

questions.stem: What is an application service map?
options: A geographic map showing where each datacenter is located
A list of every application installed on a single laptop
A view of the CIs delivering one application service
A chart of how many incidents each application had last year
questions.explanation:
Service maps show the components behind an application service — load balancers, web servers, databases — and how they connect. They're built by Service Mapping or other population methods.

Installed software lists, datacenter locations, and incident charts are different views.

questions.stem: A database server goes down. How does the CMDB help identify which business services are affected?
options: The server's description field lists every service it supports
Relationships from the server up to services show impact
The CMDB Health score shows which services are affected
Each service owner is emailed to ask whether they're affected
questions.explanation:
Impact flows through relationships from infrastructure up to application and business services, which is what impacted-service calculations use.

Descriptions aren't structured, emailing owners is slow, and health scores measure data quality.

questions.stem: How can the CMDB help change management detect conflicts?
options: By flagging other changes or blackout windows on the same or related CIs
By approving every change that touches a CI with a high health score
By blocking any change submitted outside business hours
By assigning every change to the CI's created-by user
questions.explanation:
Conflict detection checks the CIs on a change against other scheduled changes and maintenance or blackout schedules, which depends on accurate CI data.

Health scores don't approve changes, and timing and assignment rules are separate.

questions.stem: How do event management and AIOps use the CMDB?
options: They use the CMDB only to send users notifications
They replace the CMDB with their own separate inventory
They don't use CMDB data at all
Alerts are bound to CIs, so service impact can be calculated
questions.explanation:
Binding alerts to CIs lets event management group alerts and determine which services are affected.

Event management relies on the CMDB rather than replacing or ignoring it.

questions.stem: How does Vulnerability Response depend on the CMDB?
options: It only uses the CMDB to check user permissions
Vulnerabilities are matched to CIs with owners
It doesn't use the CMDB; it relies on scanner data alone
It stores vulnerabilities as CI classes in the CMDB hierarchy
questions.explanation:
Matching scanner findings to CIs tells security teams who owns the affected system and what it supports, which drives prioritization and routing.

Vulnerabilities aren't CI classes, and scanner data alone lacks ownership and business context.

questions.stem: What CMDB data does Software Asset Management rely on?
options: CSDM technical service owners only
Business service offerings and their SLAs
The CMDB Health correctness score
Discovered software installations on devices
questions.explanation:
SAM reconciles discovered software installations against entitlements, so accurate device and software data is essential.

Offerings, health scores, and service owners aren't SAM inputs.

questions.stem: Which report helps assess discovery coverage?
options: The number of knowledge articles about the CMDB
The number of users with the CMDB admin role
A list of open change requests by approver
CI counts by class and discovery source over time
questions.explanation:
Breaking down CIs by class and source shows what each tool contributes and reveals drops that suggest a broken integration.

Admin counts, change lists, and knowledge counts don't measure coverage.

questions.stem: How can a team find networks that Discovery isn't covering?
options: Compare known network ranges with the ranges in Discovery schedules
Check how many incidents mention the word "network" in their descriptions
Count how many servers each support group owns and compare the totals
Look for the CIs that have the most relationships to other CIs
questions.explanation:
