Comparing known IP ranges with what's scheduled exposes networks that are never scanned.

Ownership counts, incident text, and relationship counts don't reveal coverage gaps.

questions.stem: Which metric best shows the CMDB's value to incident management?
options: The number of times users opened the CMDB Workspace each week
The total number of CIs in the CMDB at the end of each month
The percentage of incidents with the right CI
The number of CI classes the CMDB team has created this year
questions.explanation:
If incidents reference the right CIs, the CMDB is being used to route, diagnose, and analyze. That's a usage-and-value measure.

CI counts, class counts, and page views don't show value.

questions.stem: An infrastructure team plans maintenance on a storage array. How can they see what will be affected?
options: Open it in Unified Map and follow relationships up
Ask the service desk which users have reported storage issues
Search the knowledge base for articles that mention the array
Check the array's CMDB Health score before scheduling
questions.explanation:
Following relationships from the array upward shows the servers, applications, and services that depend on it.

Knowledge articles, health scores, and past reports don't show dependencies.

questions.stem: An organization needs to find application services running on operating systems that are past end of support. What's the best approach?
options: Filter the business application list by the word "Windows" in its name
Ask each application owner to report their operating system by email
Run Discovery again and read every server record one by one
Query application services and their servers' OS versions in Query Builder
questions.explanation:
A relationship query from application services to servers and their OS versions answers this directly and can be saved and reused.

Email surveys are slow, name filters are unreliable, and reading records one by one doesn't scale.

questions.stem: Why is lifecycle reporting on hardware and software models valuable?
options: It shows which users opened CIs most frequently last month
It shows which CIs were created manually instead of being discovered
It shows which assets are nearing end of life so upgrades can be planned
It shows which Discovery patterns ran the longest last week
questions.explanation:
Lifecycle data on models — end of sale, end of support — turns the CMDB into a planning tool for upgrades and risk reduction.

Creation method, user activity, and pattern runtime are different questions.

questions.stem: During a major incident, how do impacted services help communication?
options: They close the incident once the affected services are listed
They let the service desk skip recording affected CIs
They identify which business services and users to notify
They replace the need for a major incident manager
questions.explanation:
Knowing which services are affected tells you which stakeholders to update and how widely the outage reaches.

They don't close incidents, replace roles, or remove the need to record CIs.

questions.stem: Stale CIs suddenly spike for one discovery source. What does this most likely indicate?
options: The CIs have all been certified by their owners recently
More users have started using the CMDB Workspace
The principal class list was recently expanded
That source has stopped updating its CIs
questions.explanation:
A spike concentrated on one source usually means that source broke — expired credentials, a failed schedule, or an API change.

Certification, usage, and principal classes don't cause staleness spikes.

questions.stem: Who benefits most from CMDB Query Builder's visual, no-code approach?
options: MID Servers that need instructions for running probes
End users who submit requests through the portal
External auditors who need direct database access
Analysts who need queries without scripts
questions.explanation:
Query Builder lets analysts and CMDB managers answer relationship questions without scripting.

MID Servers, auditors needing raw database access, and portal users aren't its audience.

questions.stem: Which records belong to the CSDM foundation domain?
options: Reference data like companies, locations, and groups
Application services and the infrastructure CIs that support them
Business service offerings and their service level commitments
Business applications and their portfolio lifecycle information
questions.explanation:
Foundation data is the shared reference data everything else depends on. Offerings, application services, and business applications belong to other domains.

Getting foundation data right comes first in CSDM adoption.

questions.stem: What is a technical service offering used for?
options: Defining which MID Server discovers the CIs behind a technical service
Listing the software that a business user is allowed to request from the catalog
Defining a specific IT capability with its own support and commitments
Recording the cost center that pays for each business application
questions.explanation:
Technical service offerings break a technical service into supportable units — for example, "Database hosting – Oracle – Production" — each with support groups and commitments.

Request lists, cost centers, and MID Server assignment are unrelated.

questions.stem: How does the request catalog relate to CSDM service offerings?
options: Catalog items can be linked to service offerings to show what they fulfill
The request catalog has no relationship to services anywhere in CSDM
Catalog items replace service offerings entirely once CSDM has been adopted
Service offerings can only be requested by administrators, not end users
questions.explanation:
Linking catalog items to offerings connects what users request with the services and commitments that fulfill them.

Catalog items don't replace offerings, and offerings aren't admin-only.

questions.stem: What is a dynamic CI group commonly used for in CSDM?
options: Deleting CIs automatically when they stop matching the group's query
Assigning random CIs to support groups so workloads stay balanced
Grouping CIs by query for a technical service offering
Replacing the identification rules for the CIs that are in the group
questions.explanation:
Dynamic CI groups collect CIs by query — such as all production Oracle databases — and relate them to technical service offerings, keeping support and impact accurate as CIs change.

They don't delete CIs, assign at random, or replace identification.

questions.stem: In CSDM, what does an SDLC component represent?
options: A contract with a software vendor for licenses and support
A business service that end users consume through the portal
A deployed production server that hosts the finished software
A unit of software built by a development team
questions.explanation:
SDLC components represent what development teams build and maintain, linking development work to the applications they deliver.

Servers, business services, and contracts are modeled elsewhere.

questions.stem: In the staged CSDM adoption approach, which stage typically adds technical services and technical service offerings?
options: Walk
Fly
Run
Crawl
questions.explanation:
Crawl establishes foundation data, business applications, and application services. Walk adds technical services and offerings. Run adds business services and offerings, and Fly extends further.

Stage contents vary slightly between CSDM versions, so confirm against your version.

questions.stem: Which method can populate an application service with its CIs?
options: Application services can't contain CIs
Only by importing a spreadsheet each quarter
Only by typing CI names into the service's description field
Service Mapping, tags, or a dynamic or manual definition
questions.explanation:
Application services can be populated by Service Mapping, by tags, by dynamic queries, or manually, depending on what's available.

Descriptions and periodic spreadsheets aren't population methods, and services must contain CIs to be useful.

questions.stem: Which relationship connects a business application to an application service in CSDM?
options: Runs on::Runs
Contains::Contained by
Consumes::Consumed by
Members::Member of
questions.explanation: CSDM relates business applications to the application services that deliver them with "Consumes::Consumed by". Runs on, Contains, and Members describe infrastructure relationships.

questions.stem: Why does CSDM separate business services from application services instead of using one generic service class?
options: They serve different purposes and audiences, so modeling them separately supports both
The platform can only store a limited number of records in one service class
Separating them is optional and has no effect on any platform features
Business services are always external, while application services are always internal
questions.explanation:
Business services describe what users consume. Application services describe deployed technology. Keeping them separate lets each support its own processes — service portfolio management on one side, operations on the other.

Storage limits aren't the reason, and features depend on the distinction.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a service owner and a business application owner?
options: A service owner always manages servers; an app owner always manages users
There's no difference; CSDM uses the two titles interchangeably
A service owner approves every change; an app owner approves every incident
A service owner is accountable for a service; an app owner for an application
questions.explanation:
Ownership follows the record: service owners are accountable for services and their offerings, while business application owners are accountable for the application in the portfolio.

Neither role is defined by managing servers or users, or by approving every task.

questions.stem: An identifier entry lists two criterion attributes: serial number and serial number type. How does IRE use them?
options: Both values must match for the entry to identify a CI
IRE uses whichever of the two attributes was updated more recently
Either value matching on its own is enough to identify the CI
IRE ignores the second attribute unless the first one is empty
questions.explanation:
Attributes within one identifier entry are combined: all must match. Alternatives belong in separate entries with their own priorities.

Treating them as "either" would cause false matches.

questions.stem: A higher-priority source has never reported a CI's warranty date, but a lower-priority source does. What generally happens?
options: The value stays empty until the higher-priority source reports it
IRE rejects the whole payload from the lower-priority source
IRE creates a duplicate CI so each source has its own copy
The lower-priority source can populate the empty value
questions.explanation:
Reconciliation protects values an authoritative source has set. Where it has never supplied a value, a lower-priority source can usually fill the gap, so CIs aren't left incomplete.

Rejecting payloads or creating duplicates would defeat IRE's purpose.

questions.stem: How can IRE identify a CI using the key a source system assigns to it, such as a cloud resource ID?
options: By matching the CI's description text against the payload
By the source name and source native key stored for that CI
It can't; identification only uses class identifier entries
By the CI's sys_id, which the source must look up first
questions.explanation:
IRE can match on the combination of source and its native key recorded for a CI, which is useful when sources have stable internal IDs.

Sources don't know the instance's sys_ids, and descriptions aren't identifiers.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a required attribute and an identifying attribute?
options: Required must be filled in; identifying is used to match existing CIs
There's no difference; both terms describe the same kind of attribute
Identifying attributes are set by users; required ones are set by Discovery
Required attributes are used for matching; identifying ones are optional
questions.explanation:
Required attributes drive completeness and form validation. Identifying attributes are the ones identification rules use to recognize a CI. An attribute can be one, both, or neither.

Who sets them doesn't define them.

questions.stem: In a "Depends on::Used by" relationship from an application to a database, which CI is the parent?
options: The application, which depends on the database
Neither, because relationships have no direction
The database, because it stores the data
Whichever CI was created first in the CMDB
questions.explanation:
Relationships have direction: the parent is the CI on the "Depends on" side, and the child is "Used by". Direction is what lets impact flow correctly from infrastructure up to services.

Creation order and data storage don't set direction.

questions.stem: Discovery scans are slowing production systems during business hours. What should be adjusted?
options: The principal class list for production servers
The CMDB Health weights for the affected classes
The identification rules for the scanned classes
The schedule's run time window, so scans run off-hours
questions.explanation:
Schedules control when and how long discovery runs, so moving scans to off-hours and setting a maximum run time reduces load.

Health weights, principal classes, and identification rules don't control scan timing.

questions.stem: Why configure MID Servers in a cluster?
options: So each MID Server can discover a different instance of ServiceNow
So MID Servers can calculate CMDB Health scores locally
For load balancing and failover, so discovery continues if one fails
So MID Servers can approve changes on discovered servers
questions.explanation:
Clusters spread the workload and provide redundancy for discovery and integrations.

MID Servers don't serve multiple instances this way, approve changes, or calculate health.

questions.stem: Which credential type does Discovery typically use for network switches and routers?
options: Database login credentials
Windows domain credentials
SNMP credentials
Cloud service account keys
questions.explanation: Network devices are usually discovered over SNMP. Windows credentials are for Windows hosts, database credentials for database exploration, and cloud keys for cloud APIs.

questions.stem: A source system stops reporting a device that was decommissioned. How should the integration handle records missing from the source?
options: Ignore missing records, since the CMDB should never change
Flag or retire them through governed lifecycle steps
Recreate the CIs from the previous import file each time
Delete the CIs immediately whenever they're absent from one import
questions.explanation:
A missing record may mean decommissioning or a temporary source problem. Marking or retiring through policy preserves history and avoids mass deletion after a bad import.

Instant deletion is risky, and ignoring or recreating records keeps stale data.

questions.stem: During discovery, what does the classification phase determine?
options: Which business services rely on the device
Who owns the device and which group should support it
What kind of device it is, which sets its CI class
Whether the device's data is complete enough to score well
questions.explanation:
Classification works out the device type — Windows server, Linux server, switch — from probe responses, which determines the class and which patterns run next.

Ownership, service impact, and health scoring come later or from other sources.

questions.stem: A large integration import slows the instance for users during the day. What's the recommended approach?
options: Turn off IRE for the import so that it runs much faster
Ask users to log off the instance while the import runs
Run all imports every hour so that each one is smaller
Schedule large loads off-peak and process changes in deltas
questions.explanation: Off-peak scheduling and delta loads reduce load when users need the instance. Disabling IRE trades speed for duplicates, and asking users to log off isn't practical.

questions.stem: Why should every CMDB integration have a named owner?
options: The owner becomes the owner of every CI the integration loads
Integrations can't run unless a user is logged in as the owner
Someone must notice and fix failures before data goes stale
The owner approves every CI the integration creates
questions.explanation:
Integrations break: credentials expire, APIs change. A named owner who watches run results keeps data flowing.

Integrations run unattended, don't need per-CI approval, and don't set CI ownership.

questions.stem: Agentless discovery fails against servers in a new network segment. What should be checked first?
options: Whether firewalls allow the needed ports from the MID
Whether the servers' business application owners are set
Whether CMDB Health jobs ran the previous night
Whether the class is listed as a principal class
questions.explanation:
Agentless discovery needs network access — ports such as SSH, WMI/WinRM, and SNMP — from the MID Server to targets. Blocked ports are a common cause of failure.

Ownership, principal classes, and health jobs don't affect connectivity.

questions.stem: Why set target health scores and remediation timeframes for key classes?
options: The platform blocks health scoring until targets are configured
They define what "good enough" means and make progress measurable
Targets lower the number of CIs that need to be scored
Targets let failing CIs be marked as passing automatically
questions.explanation:
Targets turn health scores into goals teams can be held to, with clear expectations for fixing failures.

Scoring works without targets, and targets don't reduce scope or override results.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a CMDB manager and a data steward?
options: There's no difference; the titles are interchangeable
Stewards configure Discovery; managers configure identification rules
The manager edits every CI personally; stewards only read reports
The manager owns the CMDB program; stewards keep specific data accurate
questions.explanation:
CMDB managers own strategy, standards, and governance. Data stewards — often within the teams that use the data — maintain quality for their classes or CIs.

Managers don't edit every CI, and the roles aren't defined by tool configuration.

questions.stem: How can the CMDB help detect unauthorized changes to servers?
options: Block Discovery from updating CIs that have open incidents
Compare discovered changes with approved changes
Lower the health score of any CI that has a change request
Delete any CI whose attributes change between two discovery runs
questions.explanation:
When discovered configuration changes don't match an approved change, that's a signal of unauthorized change worth investigating.

Deleting CIs, blocking updates, or penalizing approved changes don't detect anything.

questions.stem: When should a compliance audit use a script instead of a simple filter?
options: Always, because scripted audits run faster than filter audits
When the check is too complex to express with conditions alone
Only when the audit needs to delete failing CIs
Never, because audits can only use filter conditions
questions.explanation:
Filters cover most checks. Scripts handle logic conditions can't express, such as comparing related records. Prefer filters where possible because they're easier to maintain.

Audits shouldn't delete CIs.

questions.stem: Data quality problems are scattered across many classes. What helps find the root causes?
options: Fix each failing CI one at a time as it's reported
Ask each support group to fix whatever it notices
Disable health scoring until every class has been reviewed
Group failures by data source and class to spot the pattern
questions.explanation:
Grouping by source and class often shows that one integration or mapping causes most failures, so one fix resolves many CIs.

CI-by-CI fixes treat symptoms, and disabling scoring hides the problem.

questions.stem: Relationships between CIs that no longer exist still appear on maps. What should handle these?
options: Nothing; stale relationships don't affect maps or impact analysis
Manual deletion of every relationship each time someone notices
A new CI class to store the outdated relationships separately
Relationship staleness and cleanup rules, alongside CI lifecycle
questions.explanation:
Relationships go stale like CIs do. Governed cleanup keeps maps and impact analysis accurate.

Manual cleanup doesn't scale, new classes don't fix it, and stale relationships do distort impact.

questions.stem: Users keep manually overwriting attributes that Discovery maintains. What helps?
options: Asking users to note their changes in the CI's description field
Removing Discovery so manual values are never overwritten again
Reconciliation rules and access controls
Raising the staleness period so manual edits last longer
questions.explanation:
Reconciliation rules make the authoritative source win, and access controls limit who can edit protected fields.

Removing Discovery loses automation, descriptions don't prevent overwrites, and staleness doesn't control edits.

questions.stem: Why publish CMDB standards, such as class definitions and required attributes?
options: So everyone populating or using the CMDB follows the same rules
Because published standards make the CMDB Health score rise automatically
So the standards can replace identification and reconciliation rules
Because standards are needed before Discovery can be scheduled
questions.explanation: Shared standards keep teams and integrations consistent. They complement platform configuration rather than replacing it, and they don't change scores or Discovery on their own.

questions.stem: A new data source is being added to the CMDB. Which governance steps should happen first?
options: Give it administrator access so it can update any CMDB table
Assign it the highest priority for every attribute on every class
Load all of its data into production first and clean up duplicates later
Define its classes, identification, reconciliation priority, and an owner
questions.explanation:
Planning class mappings, identification, reconciliation precedence, and ownership before loading prevents duplicates and overwrites.

Loading first, broad admin access, or blanket top priority all create data problems.

questions.stem: A CI was archived by policy, but an audit now needs it. What's generally possible?
options: Nothing; archived CIs are permanently deleted from the instance
The CI must be rediscovered from scratch by a new Discovery run
Archived CIs can be restored, since archiving preserves them
Auditors must read the instance's database backups to find it
questions.explanation:
Archiving moves records out of active tables while keeping them, so they can be retrieved when needed. That's why archiving comes before deletion.

Rediscovery or backups aren't needed for archived data.

questions.stem: Many CIs list owners who have left the company. Why is this a governance problem?
options: Tasks and certifications route to people who can't act on them
It changes the CI's class to a retired class automatically
Former employees can still sign in and edit those CIs
The platform deletes CIs whose owners have been deactivated
questions.explanation:
Stale ownership breaks accountability: remediation tasks, certifications, and approvals go nowhere. Regular ownership checks fix it.

Deactivated users can't sign in, and CIs aren't deleted or reclassified automatically.

questions.stem: Before running a new Data Manager retire policy across thousands of servers, what's a sensible step?
options: Run it only on weekends, with no review of the scope
Preview which CIs it will affect and confirm the scope
Disable approvals so the policy finishes faster
Run it immediately and restore anything removed by mistake
questions.explanation:
Previewing the affected CIs catches a bad filter before it retires the wrong servers.

Running blind, skipping review, or removing approvals invites mistakes.

questions.stem: What role does a CMDB governance board typically play?
options: Approves every incident that references a CI before it's assigned
Runs Discovery schedules and fixes MID Server credential failures
Reviews health, sets priorities, and approves model changes
Edits CI attributes directly whenever anyone reports a data error
questions.explanation:
A governance board oversees direction: health and priorities, standards, and schema changes such as new classes.

Hands-on data edits, Discovery operations, and incident approval belong to other roles.

questions.stem: Test and development servers make production health scores look worse. What's a reasonable approach?
options: Delete all test and development servers from the CMDB entirely
Copy production attribute values onto the test servers' records
Score environments separately using inclusion rules or CMDB groups
Turn off health scoring for the entire server class until fixed
questions.explanation:
Separating environments lets each be held to appropriate standards without hiding problems.

Deleting non-production CIs loses useful data, copying values falsifies it, and disabling scoring hides everything.

questions.stem: Which servers aren't related to any application service? How can Query Builder answer this?
options: Ask each server owner which applications run on their servers
Count relationships manually on each server's form
Use a "not related" condition to application services
Filter the server list by the word "application" in its name
questions.explanation:
Query Builder can find CIs that lack a relationship, which is useful for orphan analysis and service mapping coverage.

Name filters, surveys, and manual counts are unreliable or slow.

questions.stem: A Unified Map is too cluttered to read. What helps?
options: Export the map as an image and crop it to the area of interest
Delete the relationships that make the map look busy and cluttered
Filter by relationship type, class, or depth to focus the view
Rename the CIs on the map so they have shorter display names
questions.explanation:
Filters and depth controls narrow the map to what matters for the task.

Deleting relationships destroys data, and cropping images or renaming CIs doesn't help analysis.

questions.stem: During an incident, what extra context can Unified Map show beyond relationships?
options: The personal contact details and home addresses of every user of each CI
The purchase invoices and payment history for the hardware on the map
The full source code of the applications that run on each CI
Related operational records, such as open incidents, changes, and alerts
questions.explanation:
Overlaying active incidents, recent changes, and alerts on the map helps responders spot likely causes.

Personal details, source code, and invoices aren't map overlays.

questions.stem: An analyst needs to find a specific CI quickly. Where should they start?
options: The Discovery schedule list
CMDB search in the CMDB Workspace
The identification rule list
The system log
questions.explanation: CMDB search is built for finding CIs across classes. Schedules, rules, and logs aren't CI search tools.

questions.stem: Which report most directly supports governance of business applications?
options: Business applications sorted alphabetically by name
Business applications with the longest descriptions
Business apps with no owner or lifecycle status
Business applications created on a Monday
questions.explanation: Gaps in ownership and lifecycle data show where portfolio governance is weak. Sorting, creation day, and description length don't.

questions.stem: How can CMDB data help control cloud costs?
options: By lowering the price the cloud provider charges per resource
By showing cloud resources by owner, revealing unused ones
By deleting cloud resources whenever their owner is unknown
By converting cloud resources into on-premises servers
questions.explanation:
Discovered cloud resources with owners and relationships expose idle or orphaned resources that can be cleaned up.

The CMDB doesn't set prices, and deleting or converting resources isn't its job.

questions.stem: An auditor needs the list of servers in scope for PCI DSS. How can the CMDB help?
options: Look at the CMDB Health score of the server class
Query servers related to the application services that handle card data
Ask the security team to keep a separate spreadsheet of PCI servers
List every server in the CMDB and mark them all as in scope
questions.explanation:
Relationships from payment application services to their infrastructure define the in-scope set and keep it current.

Spreadsheets drift, marking everything in scope inflates audit cost, and health scores don't define scope.

questions.stem: Which metric best shows that change management is using the CMDB?
options: The number of change approvers in the organization
The percentage of changes with affected CIs populated
The total number of changes raised each month
The average length of change descriptions
questions.explanation: If changes reference the CIs they affect, impact analysis and conflict detection can work. The other measures don't show CMDB use.

questions.stem: In CSDM, what does an information object represent?
options: A saved report built from CMDB Query Builder results for an application
A knowledge article that describes how to use a business application
A single file stored on a file server and recorded as its own CI
A type of data an application handles, used to describe its sensitivity
questions.explanation:
Information objects describe the kinds of data a business application handles — such as customer payment data — which helps assess data sensitivity and risk.

They aren't individual files, articles, or reports.

questions.stem: Why should application services carry an environment value, such as production or test?
options: So impact, support, and reporting can treat environments differently
So test environments are deleted automatically each month
Because only production services can be related to business applications
Because environment determines which MID Server discovers the service
questions.explanation:
Environment lets teams prioritize production incidents, apply different change controls, and report accurately.

It doesn't trigger deletion or MID Server selection, and non-production services can relate to business applications too.

questions.stem: What is a key benefit of adopting CSDM across ServiceNow products?
options: It's required before any CI can be created in the CMDB
It lets each team define services however it prefers
Products like ITSM, ITOM, and SPM share consistent service data
It removes the need for Discovery and service mapping entirely
questions.explanation:
A common model means service and application data means the same thing everywhere, so reporting and automation work across products.

It doesn't replace discovery, it standardizes rather than fragments, and it isn't a prerequisite for creating CIs.
